title: The Weathervane Girl
summary: Pip can feel what everyone around her wants, and she always turns to point that way, like a weathervane in the wind — agreeable, helpful, never any trouble. But a girl who always points where others want has no direction of her own, and Pip must find out what she wants before she spins herself away entirely.

chapters.title: Always Pointing Their Way
chapters.body:
Pip was twelve, and everyone said she was the easiest child in the world, the most agreeable, the most helpful — and no one, including Pip, understood that this was slowly making her disappear.

Pip had a peculiar gift, though she'd never thought of it as a gift or even noticed it as unusual: she could feel what other people wanted. Not their words — their real wants, underneath. When someone near her wanted her to agree, she felt it, like a breeze, and she turned and agreed. When someone wanted her to be cheerful, she felt that too, and became cheerful. When someone wanted her to want what they wanted — a game, a plan, an opinion — she felt the pull of it and turned that way, and wanted it too, or seemed to. Pip pointed always toward whatever the people around her wanted, the way a weathervane points always into the wind, swinging this way and that as the breezes of other people's wishes blew across her.

And it made everyone love her. She was never any trouble. She never argued, never disappointed, never wanted anything inconvenient. Whatever you wanted Pip to be, she became; whichever way you wanted her to point, she pointed. Her friends loved that she always wanted to play what they wanted to play. Her parents loved that she was so easy, so accommodating, so pleasant. Grown-ups praised her as a lovely, agreeable, selfless girl, and held her up as an example, and Pip glowed under the praise and kept on pointing whichever way the wind of others' wishes blew.

But here is the thing about a weathervane: it points in every direction, and so it has no direction of its own. And Pip was beginning, in a way she couldn't name, to feel this — to feel a strange emptiness at the center of herself, a sense that she was always spinning to face others and never, ever facing anywhere she'd chosen.

It came to her clearest in small, terrible moments. Someone would ask her, kindly, "What do you want, Pip? What would you like to do?" And Pip would open her mouth to answer — and find nothing there. A blank. Because she never knew what she wanted. She only knew what others wanted, and turned to point that way. When she tried to feel her own wishes, underneath all the borrowed ones, she found she couldn't locate them at all — as if, from years of always pointing outward, she'd worn away her own center, her own direction, her own self. She could tell you what anyone else wanted in an instant. She could not tell you one single thing that she, Pip, truly wanted, because she wasn't sure there was a she in there anymore, underneath all the spinning.

And this frightened her, quietly, more each day. She was so good at being what everyone wanted. And she was, somewhere underneath, vanishing.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Spun Away
chapters.body:
It was an old woman at the edge of the village — a strange old woman who lived alone and did not seem to want anything from anyone — who first saw what was happening to Pip.

Pip came to her door on an errand, and the old woman looked at her with sharp, clear eyes, and instead of wanting anything from Pip, she simply watched her. And Pip, standing before someone who wanted nothing from her, felt suddenly unmoored — because with no wind of wanting to point toward, she didn't know how to be, didn't know which way to face, and stood there spinning slightly, lost, like a weathervane in a dead calm.

"Ah," the old woman said quietly. "You don't know how to stand still, do you, child? When no one's telling you which way to point."

Pip didn't understand, and said so.

"You're a weathervane," the old woman said, not unkindly. "You feel what everyone wants, and you turn to point that way. Agree with this one, cheer up that one, want what the other one wants. You've done it so long and so well that you've forgotten how to point anywhere on your own. And now, when someone asks what you want, you find nothing there — because a weathervane has no direction of its own. It only ever shows which way someone else's wind is blowing." She fixed Pip with her clear eyes. "I've seen it before, child. A girl so good at being what everyone wants that she spins herself right away to nothing. Do you know what happens to a weathervane girl, in the end, if she never learns to stand still and face her own way?"

Pip shook her head, frightened.

"She disappears," the old woman said simply. "Not all at once. But a person who only ever points where others want has no self of her own to come home to. Every year there's a little less of her, worn away by all the turning, until one day she's only a spinning thing that reflects whoever's near, with nothing left in the center at all. Everyone still likes her — oh, they like her enormously, she's so agreeable — but there's no one home. She's become entirely other people's wants, and lost her own self completely." The old woman leaned close. "You're most of the way there, child. I can see it. You're nearly all wind and no vane. But not quite. There's still a little of you left in the center. And if you want to save it — if you want to be a person and not just a weathervane — you have to learn the hardest thing for someone like you. You have to learn to feel your own wants. To point your own way. Even when it's not the way the wind is blowing."

"But I can't feel my own wants," Pip whispered, and it was the truest and most frightening thing she'd ever admitted. "I've tried. There's nothing there. I only feel what everyone else wants."

"That's because you never let yourself," the old woman said. "Every time your own want started to stir, you felt someone else's want at the same time, and you turned to point at theirs instead, because theirs was safer, and pleased people, and yours might not. You've been drowning out your own direction with everyone else's for so long you've forgotten you have one. But you do. It's still there, small and quiet, under all the wind. And here's how you'll find it, child: you have to practice wanting things that no one else wants for you. You have to practice pointing your own way, especially when it disappoints someone, especially when it's inconvenient, especially when the wind is blowing hard the other way. It will feel wrong. It will feel selfish and frightening. Do it anyway. It's the only way a weathervane ever becomes a person."

chapters.title: Finding Her Own Direction
chapters.body:
Pip began to practice, and it was the hardest thing she had ever done.

She started small. The next time her friends asked what game to play, and she felt the familiar pull to want whatever they wanted, she made herself stop, and turn inward, and ask — quietly, for the first time — what do I want? And at first there was only the blank, the emptiness, the years of worn-away center. But she waited, and she resisted the pull of their wishes, and she kept asking herself, gently, until — faint and small and almost forgotten — a real want stirred. She wanted to play something else. Not what her friends wanted. Something of her own. And it terrified her to say it, because it might disappoint them, because it wasn't pointing their way. But she remembered the old woman, and she made herself say it: "Actually — I'd like to do something different today."

Her friends were surprised. One of them was even a little put out. And Pip felt the old panic, the desperate urge to spin back around and point their way and smooth it over and be agreeable again. But she held still. She held her own direction. And it turned out fine — her friends adjusted, and they did her thing, and it was good, and the world did not end because Pip had wanted something of her own.

And that was the beginning. It was slow, and it was frightening, and Pip had to practice it again and again — pointing her own way, feeling her own wants, disappointing people sometimes, being a little less endlessly agreeable. Each time, the pull to spin back toward others' wishes was strong, and each time she had to consciously resist it, and hold her own direction, and bear the discomfort of not being perfectly pleasing. But each time she did it, the small quiet self at her center grew a little stronger, a little clearer, a little more solid. She was, bit by bit, becoming a person with a direction of her own, instead of a weathervane spinning to face whoever was near.

And she made a discovery that surprised her. Learning to point her own way did not make people stop liking her — not the ones worth keeping. Her truest friends, it turned out, liked her more when she was a real person with real wants, someone who sometimes disagreed and sometimes wanted different things and was actually there, than they had when she was just an agreeable mirror of their own wishes. A weathervane is easy to be around, but there's no one to actually be friends with. A person — with her own direction, her own wants, her own self — is someone you can truly know. Pip found that her friendships got deeper, more real, once there was an actual Pip in them, and not just a reflection of whatever the others wanted.

She never lost her gift for feeling what others wanted — that stayed with her, and it made her kind and perceptive and considerate all her life. But she learned to hold it alongside her own direction, instead of letting it replace her. She could feel what others wanted and still know what she wanted, and choose — sometimes to accommodate them, freely, because she wanted to be kind, and sometimes to point her own way, because it mattered to her. The difference was that now it was a choice, made from a real center, rather than a helpless spinning toward whoever's wind blew hardest. She was a person who could choose to be generous, which is a beautiful thing — not a weathervane who couldn't do anything else, which is not generosity at all, but only emptiness that looks like it.

The old woman saw her again, a year later, and looked at her with those clear sharp eyes, and smiled. "There you are," she said. "There's someone home now. I can see you in the center, holding your own direction. You still feel everyone's wind — but you don't spin away in it anymore. You've become a person, child. A real one. That's the hardest thing a weathervane ever does."

And Pip understood, at last, the thing she'd learned. Being agreeable is easy, and being helpful is good, and feeling what others want is a gift. But a person has to have a direction of their own — has to know what they want, and be willing to point that way, even into the wind, even when it disappoints — or else they aren't really a person at all, just a spinning thing that reflects everyone and is no one. The world had praised her for being a weathervane, for having no direction of her own, for always pointing whichever way others wished. But the old woman had given her something better than praise: she'd given her back her own center, her own direction, her own self. And Pip stood in her own direction for the rest of her life — kind, and generous, and considerate, and there — a person, at last, and not a weathervane; someone who could choose to turn toward others out of love, precisely because she finally knew how to stand still and face her own way.
